power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: How physical activity and sedentary behavior relate to the subjective experience of living with a mental disorder: evidence from 4,790 university students Physical activity and subjective experience of mental disorders Come l'attività fisica e la sedentarietà si relazionano all'esperienza soggettiva del vivere con un disturbo mentale: evidenze da 4,790 studenti universitari Attività fisica ed esperienza soggettiva dei disturbi mentali positivi allo screening per almeno un disturbo mentale nei 12 mesi precedenti.

L'attività fisica è stata classificata come bassa, moderata o alta utilizzando l'International Physical Activity Questionnaire; il tempo trascorso in attività sedentarie è stato categorizzato come inferiore a 4, tra 4 e 8, oppure superiore a 8 ore al giorno.

Le associazioni con la salute mentale auto-valutata, la soddisfazione per la vita e la disperazione sono state stimate mediante regressione logistica ordinale o binaria, con aggiustamento per variabili sociodemografiche, accademiche, relative alla salute fisica, indice di massa corporea e comorbilità psichiatriche.

Rispetto a un basso livello di attività fisica, livelli moderati ed elevati di attività erano associati a una minore probabilità di hopelessness (OR moderato: 0,80; IC 95%: 0,66-0,98; OR elevato: 0,69; IC 95%: 0,58-0,83) e a una maggiore soddisfazione per la vita (OR moderato: 1,20; IC 95%: 1,03-1,40; OR elevato: 1,34; IC 95%: 1,15-1,55), ma non alla salute mentale auto-valutata dopo l'aggiustamento.

Gli studenti che trascorrevano più di 8 ore al giorno in posizione sedentaria presentavano una salute mentale auto-valutata peggiore (OR: 1,32; IC 95%: 1,13-1,54), maggiore hopelessness (OR: 1,42; IC 95%: 1,16-1,72) e minore soddisfazione per la vita (OR: 0,81; IC 95%: 0,69-0,94) rispetto a coloro che trascorrevano meno di 4 ore al giorno in attività sedentarie.

Le analisi stratificate hanno mostrato associazioni sostanzialmente coerenti tra un'elevata attività fisica e una minore hopelessness, e tra un comportamento sedentario prolungato e peggiori esiti, nei diversi strati diagnostici definiti dallo screening.
Mental health problems are increasingly recognised as a major challenge within higher education (Auerbach et al., 2016; 2018).
text.formatted: Mental health problems are increasingly recognised as a major challenge within higher education <ref type="bibr">(Auerbach et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recent international population-based studies utilizing screening instruments indicate a high prevalence of probable mental health conditions and clinically relevant symptom levels among university students (ibidem).

Specifically, published data from 2016 by the World Mental Health Survey Initiative conducted across 21 countries indicate that approximately one in five university students (20.3%) meets the diagnostic criteria for a DSM-IV mental disorder within a 12-month period (Auerbach et al., 2016).

text.text: Within this population, anxiety disorders represent the most prevalent class of conditions, followed by mood, substance use, and behavioral disorders.
Importantly, the vast majority of students reporting a 12-month disorder (83.1%) indicated symptom onset prior to university enrollment.
This suggests that higher education institutions host a substantial number of individuals who are already vulnerable to psychological difficulties before entering campus (ibidem).
Recent empirical evidence suggests that overall levels of psychological distress among young adults may also be significant.

According to a landmark global umbrella review published in 2025, 13.42% and 16.78% of university students worldwide experienced severe depressive and anxiety symptoms, respectively, while prevalence estimates rose to approximately one in three when milder or overall symptom levels were also considered (Paiva et al., 2025). text.text: Collectively, these figures point to a substantial and persistent burden of psychological distress within recent cohorts of young adults, highlighting the widespread presence of clinically significant symptoms.

text.text: The high burden of mental health problems among university students may partly reflect the convergence of academic pressures, social challenges, and major developmental transitions that characterize this stage of life (Mosconi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The high burden of mental health problems among university students may partly reflect the convergence of academic pressures, social challenges, and major developmental transitions that characterize this stage of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Mosconi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To critically analyze the psychological vulnerabilities of university students, it may be useful to situate this demographic within Jeffrey Arnett's developmental theory of emerging adulthood (Arnett, 2000).
text.formatted: To critically analyze the psychological vulnerabilities of university students, it may be useful to situate this demographic within Jeffrey Arnett's developmental theory of emerging adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arnett, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Spanning the late teens through the twenties, more specifically between the ages 18 to 25, emerging adulthood is conceptualized by Arnett as a developmental stage that is theoretically and structurally distinct from both adolescence and young adulthood.
This period is uniquely characterized by relative independence from traditional social roles and normative expectations.

Having left behind the structured dependencies of childhood and adolescence, but not yet having entered the enduring, stabilizing responsibilities of full adulthood (such as marriage, parenthood, or long-term career commitments), emerging adults operate in a transitional "roleless role" (Arnett, 2000, p.471).
text.formatted: Having left behind the structured dependencies of childhood and adolescence, but not yet having entered the enduring, stabilizing responsibilities of full adulthood (such as marriage, parenthood, or long-term career commitments), emerging adults operate in a transitional "roleless role" <ref type="bibr">(Arnett, 2000, p.471)</ref>.

text.text: This unstructured developmental space, while full of opportunity, introduces distinct psychological vulnerabilities that can compromise students' mental well-being (Arnett, 2000): • Systemic Instability and Residential Mobility: Unlike adolescence, emerging adulthood is characterized by less stable and less normatively structured living arrangements, particularly regarding residence, education, work, and family roles.
text.formatted: This unstructured developmental space, while full of opportunity, introduces distinct psychological vulnerabilities that can compromise students' mental well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arnett, 2000)</ref>: • Systemic Instability and Residential Mobility: Unlike adolescence, emerging adulthood is characterized by less stable and less normatively structured living arrangements, particularly regarding residence, education, work, and family roles.

text.text: The residential status of emerging adults is highly volatile.
This segment of the population exhibits the highest rates of residential mobility of any age group, peaking in the mid-twenties.

For college students, this often involves negotiating semiautonomous living arrangements (such as dormitories or temporary shared apartments) and frequently moving back and forth between parental and independent homes.

• Subjective Ambiguity: Subjectively, the vast majority of university-aged individuals do not feel they have fully reached adulthood, typically reporting that they feel adult "in some respects yes, in some respects no".

This sense of ambiguity arises because the criteria they value most for achieving adulthood are not demographic milestones (like marriage or graduation) but demanding, individualistic qualities of character.
Specifically, accepting responsibility for oneself, making independent decisions, and attaining financial independence are viewed as the essential markers of adulthood.
• Identity Exploration: Although emerging adulthood is that period of life that offers unparalleled opportunities to explore diverse paths in love, work, and worldviews.
These identity exploration opportunities can reasonably be expected to be stressful and isolating experiences.
Trying on different life directions often results in romantic disappointment, academic disillusionment, or the unsettling deconstruction of childhood beliefs without a clear replacement.
Furthermore, emerging adults tend to navigate these difficult transitions in isolation.

Young people in this age bracket spend significantly more of their productive and leisure time alone than almost any other demographic under forty, leaving them highly vulnerable to loneliness and depressive symptoms.

• Peak Vulnerability for High-Risk Behaviors: Driven by a combination of low parental surveillance, high sensation-seeking drives, and the absence of stabilizing adult roles, emerging adulthood represents the developmental peak for several dangerous behaviors.
Rates of substance abuse, binge drinking, unprotected sex, and reckless driving all reach their lifetime highs between the ages of 18 and 25.
Arnett theorizes that these behaviors are often explored as a way to gain novel experiences before settling down.

Neurobiological evidence (Steinberg, 2008) suggests that the higher prevalence of risk-taking behavior between the ages of 18 to 25 is potentially explained by structural and functional changes in the brain's socio emotional system, particularly the remodeling of the dopaminergic system, leading to increased reward-seeking.
text.formatted: Neurobiological evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Steinberg, 2008)</ref> suggests that the higher prevalence of risk-taking behavior between the ages of 18 to 25 is potentially explained by structural and functional changes in the brain's socio emotional system, particularly the remodeling of the dopaminergic system, leading to increased reward-seeking.

text.text: As prefrontal cortical connectivity continues to mature during emerging adulthood, the regulatory processes involved in impulse control and risktaking may remain under development throughout this period (Steinberg, 2008).
text.formatted: As prefrontal cortical connectivity continues to mature during emerging adulthood, the regulatory processes involved in impulse control and risktaking may remain under development throughout this period <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Steinberg, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It can't be ignored that risky behaviors can also act as maladaptive coping mechanisms for underlying psychological distress, exacerbating the clinical risks this population already faces.
Ultimately, recognizing university students as emerging adults highlights that their psychological distress is not merely a collection of isolated clinical symptoms.

Instead, it is deeply rooted in a highly volatile, unstructured, and often lonely developmental transition, which may help explain the heightened vulnerability to mental health difficulties during the university years.

In addition to these shared developmental challenges, individuals in higher education must contend with a unique set of student-specific demands that distinguish their experience from the broader non-student demographic.

University students are exposed to sustained cognitive demands, performance pressure, and psychosocial stressors that have been associated with elevated rates of anxiety and depressive symptoms (Wunsch et al., 2021).
text.formatted: University students are exposed to sustained cognitive demands, performance pressure, and psychosocial stressors that have been associated with elevated rates of anxiety and depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Wunsch et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In a qualitative review, Hurst et al. (2012) identify seven categories amongst the most commonly reported stressors.
text.formatted: In a qualitative review, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hurst et al. (2012)</ref> identify seven categories amongst the most commonly reported stressors.

text.text: These include: academic demands, interpersonal relationships (mostly family-related stressors), expectations, financial and material resources, environmental factors, diversity-related challenges and life transitions (Hurst et al., 2012).
text.formatted: These include: academic demands, interpersonal relationships (mostly family-related stressors), expectations, financial and material resources, environmental factors, diversity-related challenges and life transitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hurst et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The consequences of this mental health burden extend across multiple areas of students' lives, including quality of life, social functioning, academic performance, and the risk of self-harm and suicidal behaviours (Wilks et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The consequences of this mental health burden extend across multiple areas of students' lives, including quality of life, social functioning, academic performance, and the risk of self-harm and suicidal behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Wilks et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The World Health Organization (2016) places suicide as the second leading cause of death worldwide for individuals aged 15-29.
Empirical evidence from a global meta-analysis indicates that suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) are alarmingly common in this demographic (Mortier et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence from a global meta-analysis indicates that suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) are alarmingly common in this demographic <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Mortier et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, pooled lifetime prevalence estimates show that nearly one in four college students (22.3%) experience suicidal ideation, while 6.1% formulate a suicide plan, and 3.2% make a suicide attempt.
It must be said that prevalence estimates of STB amongst college students vary widely (Mortier et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It must be said that prevalence estimates of STB amongst college students vary widely <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Mortier et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the exact magnitude of suicide thoughts and behavior among college students around the world is currently unknown (ibidem).
In the Italian university system, a systematic review estimated suicide risk among students at 6.1% (Gambolò et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In the Italian university system, a systematic review estimated suicide risk among students at 6.1% <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gambolò et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the progression from thought to action within this population is highly critical: approximately 40% to 45% of students who experience suicidal ideation also report formulating a plan, and about 20% progress to an active suicide attempt. (Mortier et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the progression from thought to action within this population is highly critical: approximately 40% to 45% of students who experience suicidal ideation also report formulating a plan, and about 20% progress to an active suicide attempt. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Mortier et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To contextualize this data, Rory O'Connor's integrated motivational-volition model of suicidal behavior (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018) provides a "ideation to action" framework by splitting the suicidal process into two distinct stages.
text.formatted: To contextualize this data, Rory O'Connor's integrated motivational-volition model of suicidal behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref> provides a "ideation to action" framework by splitting the suicidal process into two distinct stages.

text.text: First, the motivational phase explains how suicidal thoughts develop.
Under intense stress, students can experience severe feelings of defeat.
If they perceive no escape from this psychological pain, they enter a state of inescapable entrapment, which acts as the direct cognitive bridge to suicidal ideation (ibidem).
text.formatted: If they perceive no escape from this psychological pain, they enter a state of inescapable entrapment, which acts as the direct cognitive bridge to suicidal ideation <ref type="bibr">(ibidem)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, research has shown that entrapment is a robust predictor of depression, and this association seems to be partly mediated by hopelessness (Choi & Shin, 2023).
text.formatted: Crucially, research has shown that entrapment is a robust predictor of depression, and this association seems to be partly mediated by hopelessness <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Choi & Shin, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the volitional phase governs the critical transition from thoughts to actual behavior.
This transition is moderated by volitional moderators such as access to methods and specific personological traits (e.g. impulsivity, fearlessness about death).

Distinguishing between these two phases is clinically essential, as it explains the stark epidemiological discrepancy between the large percentage of students who experience lifetime suicidal thoughts and the much smaller, distinct subgroup who progress to active suicide attempts (Mortier et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Distinguishing between these two phases is clinically essential, as it explains the stark epidemiological discrepancy between the large percentage of students who experience lifetime suicidal thoughts and the much smaller, distinct subgroup who progress to active suicide attempts <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Mortier et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Even though suicide is the most extreme outcome of mental health struggles, its risk must be carefully evaluated and managed by mental health professionals, especially in university settings.
To this day, suicide remains a heavily stigmatized topic, often due to the fear that discussing it openly might trigger copycat behaviors (Romaniello, 2021).
text.formatted: To this day, suicide remains a heavily stigmatized topic, often due to the fear that discussing it openly might trigger copycat behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Romaniello, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, the impact of suicide goes far beyond the individual, deeply affecting families, friends, and entire communities.
As a result, identifying risk and protective factors that may inform effective public health action represents an important priority.
Against this background, physical activity has emerged as a promising factor associated with mental health and well-being.
There is an increasing amount of evidence documenting the beneficial impacts of physical activity (PA) on mental health (MH) (Biddle, 2016; Ahsan & Abualait, 2025).
text.formatted: There is an increasing amount of evidence documenting the beneficial impacts of physical activity (PA) on mental health (MH) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Biddle, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ahsan & Abualait, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Sedentary behaviour has also emerged as an important correlate of mental health, with systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently showing associations between greater sedentary time and poorer psychological well-being, higher levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, and an increased risk of other common mental disorders (Firth et al., 2020; Hallgren et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Zhai et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Sedentary behaviour has also emerged as an important correlate of mental health, with systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently showing associations between greater sedentary time and poorer psychological well-being, higher levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, and an increased risk of other common mental disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Firth et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hallgren et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Liu et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhai et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Physical activity and sedentariness have been extensively investigated in relation to mental health and psychological well-being.
The current state of research seems to suggest that physical activity may serve both therapeutic and preventive functions.

A substantial body of evidence indicates that physically active individuals experience lower levels of depression, anxiety, and psychological distress, while exercise interventions have been shown to improve symptoms of depression and other common mental disorders (Kang et al., 2020; Ross et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023).

Exercise interventions may also provide effective treatment for stress-related disorders, psychotic disorders, and ADHD (Firth et al., 2020).

text.text: In addition to its therapeutic role, regular physical activity has also been associated with a lower risk of developing depression and anxiety disorders altogether.

This protective effect exhibits a distinct dose-response relationship, whereby higher volumes of physical activity are associated with a progressively lower risk of developing depressive symptoms (Dishman et al., 2021; McDowell et al., 2019).

text.text: The same holds true for anxiety disorders.
Engaging in physical activity protects against anxiety symptoms and disorders. (McDowell et al., 2019).

It should be noted that there is now some evidence that muscular strength and resistance training are just as protective against mental illness (Firth et al., 2020).

text.text: Against this background, the relevance of physical activity and sedentariness may be particularly pronounced in higher education settings because they represent modifiable behaviours that can be targeted through large-scale prevention and health promotion initiatives.
The relationship between physical activity and mental health appears more complex than a simple linear association.

Evidence suggests that the magnitude and direction of associations may vary according to certain moderators which may play a role in psychological outcomes: intensity (low, moderate, vigorous), type (yoga, strength training, cardio, stretching), contact with nature, frequency and context (Eather et al., 2023; Lubans et al., 2016; Mahindru et al., 2023; Rossi et al., 2024).

text.text: These findings suggest that the relationship between physical activity and mental health may be more nuanced than commonly assumed, with benefits potentially emerging for specific psychological domains rather than across all indicators of mental health.

Additional evidence suggests that the context in which physical activity occurs may also be relevant, with leisure-time physical activity appearing particularly beneficial for promoting mental health and reducing mental ill-health (Teychenne et al., 2026).

text.text: Conversely, when physical activity occurs in poorly designed or negative environments, it can actively undermine psychological wellbeing.
Compulsive exercise provides an interesting example of this potential tension.
Compulsive exercise is a concept first described in the 1970s.
It is defined by an intense urge to train, which leads to uncontrollable and excessive workouts (Lichtenstein et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It is defined by an intense urge to train, which leads to uncontrollable and excessive workouts <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lichtenstein et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As the authors explain, this behavior often has negative effects, including physical injuries and strained social relationships.
Although it is widely discussed, compulsive exercise is not yet officially recognized as a mental disorder in diagnostic manuals like the DSM or the ICD.

Interestingly, according to Weinstein et al (2015), as cited in Lichtenstein et al., 2017, a positive link between compulsive exercise and depressive symptoms has been observed in both professional and amateur athletes.

text.text: Thus, the relationship between physical activity and mental health cannot simply be reduced to a "more is better" model.
However, understanding the relationship between physical activity and mental health requires consideration of how mental health itself is conceptualized and measured.

Much of the literature has focused on psychopathological symptoms and diagnostic outcomes, which provide important information about the presence and severity of mental disorders but may not fully capture individuals' broader psychological experience.
In clinical psychology and psychiatry, there is a growing debate about how we should understand mental health conditions.
Traditional psychiatric approaches, heavily influenced by biological reductionism, often view mental disorders as simple brain dysfunctions or chemical imbalances (Liccione.
In this view, diagnosing a patient means matching their behaviors with a static category in manuals like the DSM.
Clinical psychology defines this diagnostic process as "nomothetic" which stands in stark contrast to the alternative, the "idiographic" approach.

While an idiographic focus concentrates on the irreplaceable specificity and uniqueness of the individual, it risks producing clinical formulations that are unscientific, non-verifiable, and impossible to generalize; conversely, a purely nomothetic approach seeks universal laws and recurrent patterns but risks equating the patient to an inanimate object (Dazzi et al., 2009).
text.formatted: While an idiographic focus concentrates on the irreplaceable specificity and uniqueness of the individual, it risks producing clinical formulations that are unscientific, non-verifiable, and impossible to generalize; conversely, a purely nomothetic approach seeks universal laws and recurrent patterns but risks equating the patient to an inanimate object <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dazzi et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In doing so, as Liccione (2013) argues, this nosographical categorization fails to see the unique person (a "Who") and instead treats the individual as a mere physical "thing" (Körper).
When a clinical diagnosis like depression is applied, the patient's individual history is often lost in favor of a general label.
This risk of turning a person into a static category connects directly with the clinical perspective of Vittorio Lingiardi in his work Diagnosi e destino (2018).
Lingiardi is an Italian psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and Full Professor of Clinical Psychology at Sapienza University of Rome.
He argues that a diagnosis should never be a deterministic "destiny" or a label that defines a person's entire identity.
Instead, it must serve as a dynamic map within the therapeutic relationship, helping clinicians understand the patient's unique way of suffering.
Therefore, to truly understand mental illness, we must look beyond objective symptom severity and focus on the patient's lived experience.
In this context, integrating subjectivity into diagnostic assessment does not imply an extreme, unscientific subjectivism, but rather serves to "give meaning to the diagnosis (Dazzi et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In this context, integrating subjectivity into diagnostic assessment does not imply an extreme, unscientific subjectivism, but rather serves to "give meaning to the diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dazzi et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: It's this very same philosophy that has helped shape the Psychodiagnostic Manual (PDM-2), of which he and Nancy McWilliams are authors.
The PDM-2 stands in direct contrast to the DSM's descriptive nosology.
Unlike the DSM, which groups disorders based on checklists of observable symptoms, the PDM adopts a psychodynamically oriented, dimensional framework.
It evaluates the depth of personality organization, mental capacities, and the subjective experience of symptoms.

The clinical philosophy behind this manual stands in contrast to the traditional medical-positivist model -which relies on generalizable theoretical constructs and views subjectivity as redundant or even detrimental -as well as classical psychoanalysis, which historically rejected descriptive categorization to the point of treating "diagnosis" as a dirty word (Dazzi et al., 2009).

text.text: Against this background, the symptom-reduction focus of the previous literature reviewed above reveals a significant conceptual and clinical limitation in how the relationship between movement and mental health has been approached.

Research in university settings has predominantly examined how physical activity and sedentary behavior relate to symptoms of depression, anxiety, and psychological distress in student populations as a whole.
In other words, conceptually most studies have operated under a reductionist model that treats the student's body merely as a physical object (Körper).
In this view, physical activity is analyzed almost mechanically, focusing on how exercise can reduce score severity on standard symptom checklists of anxiety and depression.

This symptom-centered approach mirrors the descriptive, category-based models of the DSM, which have been criticized by clinicians like Vittorio Lingiardi for ignoring the patient's subjective experience.

By focusing only on biological and chemical mechanisms, past research has conceptually detached physical activity from the lived body (Leib), the actual vehicle of our actions, personal meanings, and relationship with the world (Liccione, 2013).

Comparatively less attention has been devoted to students experiencing mental disorders, for whom the relevant question may concern not only whether physical activity and reduced sedentary time are associated with lower condition-specific symptom levels, but also whether they relate to broader aspects of well-being.
This reductionist blind spot may also explain many of the inconsistencies and contradictory findings observed in the existing literature, we discussed previously.

A simple count of active minutes or step counts cannot distinguish between a student engaging in joyful, autonomous leisure-time exercise which is consistently linked to better mental health (Teychenne et al., 2026) and a student engaging in rigid, compulsive, or compensatory movement driven by psychological distress (Lichtenstein et al., 2017).

text.text: Because the reductionist approach aggregates these vastly different subjective experiences into the same quantitative data, the underlying clinical realities might be obscured, leading to mixed and confusing statistical outcomes.

Furthermore, by focusing strictly on symptom-reduction checklists, past studies might miss the broader, positive changes in how active students evaluate their lives (life satisfaction) or view their future (hopelessness), even when their baseline clinical symptoms remain unchanged.

Therefore, shifting the focus from objective symptom severity to the subjective experience of functioning is not just a theoretical preference; but it might be a methodological necessity to resolve the contradictions in current psychiatric and sports science literature.

To address this issue, contemporary research increasingly recognizes that standardized measures of symptom severity often fail to capture subjective experience of living with a mental disorder, as comparable scores may correspond to markedly different personal circumstances and perceptions (Correll et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To address this issue, contemporary research increasingly recognizes that standardized measures of symptom severity often fail to capture subjective experience of living with a mental disorder, as comparable scores may correspond to markedly different personal circumstances and perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Correll et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As Correll and colleagues (2025) point out, relying strictly on categorical, symptom-based checklists carries the risk of dehumanizing the patient by reducing their complex existence to a mere checklist of deficits.
To address this limitation, contemporary clinical psychiatry is shifting its focus toward patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) that capture dimensions beyond simple symptom reduction.

Within this framework, a crucial distinction must be made between "functional recovery" defined as the observable ability to perform daily, social, and academic activities, and "personal recovery" (Correll et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Within this framework, a crucial distinction must be made between "functional recovery" defined as the observable ability to perform daily, social, and academic activities, and "personal recovery" <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Correll et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As Correll and colleagues explain, personal recovery represents a deeply subjective, unique process of building a satisfying, hopeful, and contributing life, even within the limitations potentially caused by a mental health condition.
For university students experiencing psychological difficulties, clinical recovery is about much more than just lowering a symptom score on a questionnaire.
The most relevant question is whether movement behaviors relate not only to functional performance but also to these deeper, subjective aspects of personal recovery.

By failing to investigate how physical activity and sedentary behavior relate to these broader, subjective dimensions, such as self-rated mental health, life satisfaction, and hopelessness, the existing literature misses the opportunity to evaluate movement as a transdiagnostic resource that supports the student's overall sense of agency and future outlook.

Self-rated mental health represents an individual's subjective evaluation of their own mental health status and has been shown to correlate with objective measures of mental health such as symptom severity, functional impairment, and broader health outcomes (McAlpine et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Self-rated mental health represents an individual's subjective evaluation of their own mental health status and has been shown to correlate with objective measures of mental health such as symptom severity, functional impairment, and broader health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(McAlpine et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A debate persists in the literature regarding the scientific validity of this construct.

Although self-rated mental health is moderately correlated with standardized measures of distress and depression, a significant proportion of people who meet the clinical criteria for a mental disorder still evaluate their own mental health positively.

Specifically, evidence shows that despite experiencing active symptoms or having a formal medical diagnosis for conditions such as major depression or anxiety disorders, about half of these individuals rate their overall mental health as good, very good, or excellent (Jang et al., 2015; Mawani & Gilmour, 2010; as cited in McAlpine et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Specifically, evidence shows that despite experiencing active symptoms or having a formal medical diagnosis for conditions such as major depression or anxiety disorders, about half of these individuals rate their overall mental health as good, very good, or excellent <ref type="bibr">(Jang et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mawani & Gilmour, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">as cited in McAlpine et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Some researchers view SRMH as an indicator of how well individuals recognize their own symptoms as signs of a mental illness.
From this perspective, individuals who meet the criteria for a mental disorder but still rate their mental health positively are often described as "mismatched" or incongruent (ibidem).
From a traditional, symptom-based psychiatric perspective, this gap is seen as a cognitive mismatch or a lack of clinical insight.
The assumption is that these individuals simply fail to recognize their symptoms as signs of a mental illness.
In other words, they are indeed rating their mental health "better than it actually is" because they are either in denial or lack the literacy to understand their clinical condition.
Traditional frameworks treat standardized DSM criteria and symptom scales as the objective 'gold standard' for mental illness.
From this perspective, because self-rated mental health (SRMH) does not always align strongly with these clinical measures, it is often dismissed as an invalid indicator.
However, McAlpine et al. (2018) offer a compelling alternative explanation.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">McAlpine et al. (2018)</ref> offer a compelling alternative explanation.

text.text: They argue that these individuals are not wrong or in denial about their symptoms.
Rather, it could also be they do not define their overall mental health solely by the presence of clinical symptoms.
An individual experiencing sadness or sleep issues after a breakup or an academic challenge may acknowledge these struggles but view them as normal and not symptoms of a psychiatric disease.
Because they factor in these temporary life circumstances, they still evaluate their overall mental health positively.
A student might actively screen positive for generalized anxiety but also have strong social support and excellent coping strategies.
They recognize their anxiety, but because they are successfully navigating their life, they still rate their overall mental health as "good".

In other words, this perspective challenges the assumption that standardized, symptom-based scales are completely objective measures of psychiatric conditions, highlighting instead that the boundaries between health and clinical disorder are highly amorphous.
Many common symptoms of psychological distress represent expected, natural human reactions to challenging life events rather than signs of permanent pathology.

Because individuals naturally incorporate these personal life circumstances into their emotional selfassessments, subjective appraisals of mental health (SRMH) may carry the same validity and clinical relevance as categorical clinical measures that rely on arbitrary scale cut-off points.

Ultimately, self-rated mental health emerges not as an imperfect proxy for objective pathology, but as a highly valid, context-sensitive appraisal of an individual's emotional status (McAlpine et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Ultimately, self-rated mental health emerges not as an imperfect proxy for objective pathology, but as a highly valid, context-sensitive appraisal of an individual's emotional status <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(McAlpine et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This demonstrates that psychological well-being is defined by much more than the mere absence of clinical symptoms, as individuals actively evaluate their mental state in relation to their unique life circumstances.

Shifting the focus to this subjective appraisal of functioning paves the way for examining broader cognitive dimensions of subjective well-being, most notably how students evaluate their overall satisfaction with life.

Life satisfaction or satisfaction with life constitutes the cognitive-judgmental component of subjective well-being, distinguishing itself from the positive and negative affect that represent the emotional, or affective, dimensions of psychological well-being.
Conceptually, life satisfaction is defined as a global assessment of an individual's quality of life according to their own self-selected standards (Diener et al., 1985).
text.formatted: Conceptually, life satisfaction is defined as a global assessment of an individual's quality of life according to their own self-selected standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diener et al., 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than relying on externally imposed criteria chosen by a researcher, such as objective health markers or material wealth, this evaluative process centers entirely on the individual's subjective judgment.
An individual assesses their satisfaction by comparing their unique life circumstances against a standard that they set for themselves (ibidem).
A key strength of this conceptualization is captured by the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), designed by Ed Diener and colleagues (1985), which operates as a "narrow-band" instrument.
text.formatted: A key strength of this conceptualization is captured by the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), designed by Ed <ref type="bibr">Diener and colleagues (1985)</ref>, which operates as a "narrow-band" instrument.

text.text: Unlike other scales that include affective elements like zest, apathy, or loneliness, the SWLS is strictly focused on cognitive appraisal.

Consequently, evaluating life satisfaction provides a vital, subjective window into student functioning and personal recovery, capturing a vital dimension of well-being that symptom-based clinical checklists cannot measure

Another construct of clinical relevance is hopelessness, commonly defined as the presence of negative expectations regarding the future and perceived inability to influence desired outcomes (Abramson, Metalsky, & Alloy, 1989).
text.formatted: Another construct of clinical relevance is hopelessness, commonly defined as the presence of negative expectations regarding the future and perceived inability to influence desired outcomes (Abramson, <ref type="bibr">Metalsky, & Alloy, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: In their reformulated hopelessness theory of depression, Abramson and colleagues (1989) conceptualize hopelessness not merely as a symptom of psychological distress, but as a proximal sufficient cause that directly triggers a specific subtype of depressive symptoms.
text.formatted: In their reformulated hopelessness theory of depression, <ref type="bibr">Abramson and colleagues (1989)</ref> conceptualize hopelessness not merely as a symptom of psychological distress, but as a proximal sufficient cause that directly triggers a specific subtype of depressive symptoms.

text.text: Specifically, this cognitive construct is defined by the coexistence of two core expectations: a negative outcome expectancy, where an individual believes that highly desired outcomes will not occur or that highly aversive ones will occur, and a helplessness expectancy, where the individual believes that no response in their personal repertoire can change the likelihood of these outcomes.
The theory distinguishes between generalized hopelessness, which occurs when these negative expectations span many areas of life, and circumscribed pessimism, which is restricted to a limited domain.

Taken together -self-rated mental health, satisfaction with life, and hopelessness -provide complementary perspectives on individuals' overall appraisal of their current mental state, their global evaluation of their lives, and their outlook on the future (Kjell & Diener, 2021; McAlpine et al., 2018; Yip & Cheung, 2006).

It involves a wide network of universities and AFAM institutions (Higher Education in Art, Music and Dance) working to promote the well-being of everyone who populates these environments (Mosconi et al., 2026).

text.text: To transform the university environment requires a fundamental shift in its narrative.

The Health Mode On framework is built upon seven core guiding principles designed to redefine educational spaces while actively seeking to mitigate the systemic stressors historically associated with higher education (HMO, 2025): 1.

People, Not Users: Rather than viewing students as mere metrics, targets, or matriculation numbers, this principle recognizes them as unique individuals with distinct aspirations, challenges, and needs.
Educational institutions must prioritize active listening and welcoming spaces to ensure that the university experience fosters both personal and social growth.
Continuous Experiences, Not Isolated Projects: Fostering student well-being requires a continuous, harmonious, and long-term institutional commitment rather than temporary, short-term initiatives.
The focus must remain on cultivating sustained and meaningful relationships between educators and students.
Relational Quality, Not Bureaucratic Procedures: In every institutional touchpoint, relational depth must take precedence over rigid administrative procedures.
This human-centric approach is essential to honor the unique nuances of each individual, supporting them holistically through their developmental journey.
Holistic Growth, Not Performance-Driven Metrics: Education is a developmental process designed to enrich and shape personal and social growth.

Academic achievement should not be reduced to numeric grades; rather, true success is defined by a student's capacity to navigate challenges with emotional balance, resilience, and conscious self-determination.

Autonomy and Choice, Not Forced Paths: Rather than imposing highly constrained, predetermined paths that fuel anxiety and uncertainty, the university must provide students with the space to identify their own needs, encouraging autonomous and deliberate life choices.
By combining different tracking tools, this project looks at both students' mental health symptoms and their physical lifestyle habits, which help design personalized prevention plans.

To bring together typically disconnected campus services like counseling, sports centers, and local clinics, the Health Mode On (HMO) project and its expansion, Health Mode On Plus (HMO+), combine rigorous screening with a step-by-step, multi-team support model (Vigezzi et al., 2026).

text.text: Therefore, the current study belongs to the first phase of the HMO project.
This phase has three main goals (ibidem): • Measure distress: Find out how common psychological distress and risky habits are among students and identify what causes them.
• Connect services: Design a flexible counseling model that links campus support directly with local specialist clinics.
• Train staff: Set up a Virtual Academy to train university staff and student tutors.
The second phase, HMO+, expands this work by: • Following up with individual students over a 12-month period.
• Improving the online counseling and triage (student sorting) platform.
• Using objective tracking tools for physical activity and diet.
• Testing a short, online Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) program specifically for anxiety.
Ultimately, both projects aim to create practical, fair, and scalable mental health support systems on campus.
Within this framework, assessing students is not just about gathering statistics.
It is a tool used to constantly improve campus services and target help directly to those who need it most (Vigezzi, 2026).

text.text: The current study describes patterns of physical activity and sedentary behaviour and examines their associations with self-rated mental health, life satisfaction, and hopelessness among nearly 4,800 university students who screened positive for at least one mental disorder.
It also analyzes whether these associations vary across major categories of mental disorders.

The broader aim is to extend current evidence beyond symptom-based outcomes and provide a more comprehensive understanding of how movement behaviours relate to students' subjective experience of living with a mental disorder.
This study used data from Benessere in Campus, a university-wide mental health survey conducted at the University of Pavia (Italy) as part of the Health Mode On research project.
The study design can be described as a cross-sectional study.
As opposed to a longitudinal study that follows the participants over time, a cross-sectional study collects data from participants at one single point in time.
Details regarding study design, recruitment procedures, survey administration, and ethical approval have been reported on Vigezzi et al. (2026).

text.text: Recruitment leverages institutional mailing lists and learning platforms, amplified by student associations and institutional channels.
To mitigate non-response and attrition, the survey is modular and concise, staged reminders are deployed, and communications emphasize benefits and confidentiality.

Mitigation of non-response bias therefore relies not only on weighting at the analysis stage, but also on recruitment design, institutional dissemination, student engagement, and a questionnaire structure intended to support participation and completion (ibidem).

For the present study, we restricted the sample to students who screened positive for the presence of at least one mental disorder in the 12 months before taking part in the survey, according to standard WMH-ICS algorithms based on validated screening instruments derived from the Composite International Diagnostic Interview Screening Scales (CIDI-SC).
As exposures, we considered physical activity and sedentary behaviour.

Physical Mental disorders were identified using WMH-ICS scoring algorithms and grouped into major diagnostic categories, including mood disorders, anxiety disorders, traumarelated disorders, eating disorders, substance-related and addictive disorders, and other mental disorders (Vigezzi et al., 2026).

text.text: Diagnostic groups were not mutually exclusive because participants could screen positive for multiple conditions.
The outcomes of interest were self-rated mental health, life satisfaction, and hopelessness.
Self-rated mental health was assessed using a single-item question asking participants to rate their overall mental health on a five-point scale (poor, fair, good, very good, and excellent).
Life satisfaction was measured using the three-item Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS-3) and analysed in quartiles.
Hopelessness was assessed using the fouritem version of the Beck Hopelessness Scale and dichotomised using a cut-off score of ≥6.

Physical activity and sedentary behaviour patterns were described across 12-month diagnostic groups, including comorbidity (i.e., two or more disorders), mood disorders, anxiety disorders, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) (brief screening), suicidal dimension, and eating disorders.
Differences between groups were verified through a Chi-square test.

Associations between each exposure (i.e., physical activity levels and sedentary behaviour) and each outcome were examined using separate logistic regression models, according to the outcomes distribution.
Reference category was "low level" for physical activity, and "<4 hours/day" for sedentary behaviour.

text.text: Binary logistic regression was used for hopelessness, whereas ordinal logistic regression models were used for self-rated mental health and life satisfaction.

Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were estimated through three sequential models: i) an unadjusted model; ii) further adjusted for sociodemographic, academic characteristics, and family contextual factors (sex, age, foreign student status, year of study, academic macro-area, academic delay, parental education, and family economic situation); iii) further fully adjusted for body mass index (BMI), self-rated physical health, and psychiatric comorbidity (presence of two or more mental disorders).

To explore potential heterogeneity across the considered groups of mental conditions during the past 12 months, stratified fully adjusted models were performed for each major diagnostic category according to presence or absence.
All analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4.

text.text: Based on physical activity reported over the previous seven days, 19.6% of students were classified as having low activity levels, 32.1% as having moderate levels, and 48.3% as having high levels according to IPAQ categories.
Over the same seven-day period, the average daily time spent sitting was less than four hours for 29.8% of participants, between four and eight hours for 48.5%, and more than eight hours for 21.7%.
Patterns of physical activity and sedentary behaviour differed across mental health screening categories.
Among students with low physical activity, 66.1% screened positive for two or more mental disorders, compared with 61.8% of those with moderate activity and 61.9% of those with high activity.

The proportions screening positive for mood disorders, anxiety disorders, and suicidal behaviours were lower across increasing physical activity categories, decreasing from 34.4% to 28.9%, from 50.0% to 39.2%, and from 29.2% to 24.5%, respectively.

Conversely, the proportion screening positive for an eating disorder was slightly higher among students with high than low physical activity (42.2% vs 39.0%), while little variation was observed for PTSD.

Regarding sedentary behaviour, the proportions screening positive for two or more mental disorders, mood disorders, anxiety disorders, and suicidal behaviours tended to be higher among students reporting longer average daily sitting time.

The clearest differences were observed for anxiety disorders, increasing from 38.2% among students sitting for less than 4 hours per day to 48.8% among those sitting for more than 8 hours, and for suicidal behaviours, increasing from 23.8% to 30.0%.

In contrast, the proportion screening positive for an eating disorder was lower among students reporting more than 8 hours of sitting per day than among those reporting less than 4 hours (38.1% vs 43.0%), while differences in PTSD screening results were limited.

In this large sample of university students who screened positive for at least one mental disorder in the 12 months before the survey, higher physical activity and lower sedentary behaviour were associated with more favourable profiles across the mental health outcomes assessed.

Specifically, higher physical activity was associated with lower hopelessness and greater life satisfaction, whereas prolonged sedentary behaviour was associated with poorer self-rated mental health, greater hopelessness, and lower life satisfaction.

These associations remained after adjustment for several confounders, including sociodemographic, academic, behavioural, and clinical factors, suggesting that movement behaviours may represent relevant correlates of specific aspects of well-being among students screening positive for mental health conditions.
Our findings are broadly consistent with the extensive literature linking physical activity to better mental health outcomes.

Previous reviews, systematic reviews, and metaanalyses have shown that physically active individuals report lower levels of depression, anxiety, and psychological distress, while exercise interventions can improve symptoms across a range of common mental disorders (Firth et al., 2020; Ross et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023).

text.text: However, unlike previous research, which has largely focused on symptom-based measures, our findings suggest that physical activity may also be associated with a more favourable subjective experience of living with a mental disorder.
Notably, physical activity was not associated uniformly with the three subjective outcomes examined among students who had already screened positive for at least one mental disorder.

After full adjustment, higher physical activity remained associated with lower hopelessness and greater life satisfaction, whereas the association with self-rated mental health was attenuated to the null.

This differential pattern suggests that, within a population already experiencing a substantial mental health burden, physical activity is not simply associated with a more favourable global appraisal of mental health.
Rather, its association appears to be more evident for specific dimensions of subjective experience, particularly how individuals evaluate their lives and future prospects.

These findings support the distinction between the presence of a probable mental disorder and the broader subjective experience of living with it, and highlight the value of considering life satisfaction and hopelessness alongside global self-rated mental health. text.text: The key neurobiological pathways outlined by the authors are the following: 1.

Neural Plasticity, Growth Factors, and Brain Structure Exercise acts as a major catalyst for structural and functional brain remodeling, reversing the cell atrophy and limbic structure degradation linked to mental disorders (ibidem): • Hippocampal and Grey Matter Growth: Montgomery and Grant report that daily physical activity can modify up to 82% of the total grey matter in the brain, with aerobic exercise shown to actively prevent volume decline in the hippocampus over a single year.
It also strengthens neural connectivity between the prefrontal cortex (PFC), amygdala (AMY), and hippocampus, which helps blunt the fear/arousal response to stressful stimuli.
Aerobic training also increases grey and white matter volume in the anterior cingulate cortex (ibidem).

• Neurotrophic Signaling (BDNF and NGF): As explained by the authors, brainderived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) support synaptic plasticity, cell genesis, and neuronal survival.
Individuals with mood disorders display low baseline levels of these factors, which elevate with chronic exercise (ibidem).

• Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) and Angiogenesis (IGF-1 and VEGF): Physical exercise stimulates the peripheral release of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) from the liver, muscles, and blood cells (ibidem).
These proteins cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to enhance neurogenesis, blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), and LTP, the primary synaptic mechanism for learning and memory (ibidem).

• Anti-Aging Protein Expression (Klotho): according to the authors exercise also stimulates the expression of Klotho, a pleiotropic protein that improves cognitive function, enhances stem-cell-driven regenerative responses, and confers resistance to oxidative stress (ibidem).
Skeletal muscle acts as a secretory endocrine organ, releasing proteins (myokines) and metabolites that cross the blood-brain barrier to trigger neuroplasticity (ibidem).

• Cathepsin B (CTSB): The authors explain that protease is upregulated in skeletal muscle and brain following exercise, crossing the BBB to directly stimulate BDNF mRNA, BDNF protein, and doublecortin (a neuroprotective protein promoting neuronal migration).
• Irisin and the PGC-1α Pathway: Endurance exercise triggers PGC-1α (a co-activator of mitochondrial biogenesis), which upregulates FNDC5 gene expression in the hippocampus.
This FNDC5/irisin cascade directly stimulates BDNF synthesis.
Boosting brain FNDC5 has been shown to rescue synaptic plasticity and memory impairments in models of Alzheimer's disease (ibidem).

• Lactate and Ketones (b-HB): Prolonged aerobic exercise elevates bhydroxybutyrate b-HB), a ketone body that crosses the BBB via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) to stimulate hippocampal BDNF expression (ibidem).
Similarly, lactate accumulates during acute exercise and crosses the BBB via MCTs.

Astrocytic lactate is transported to neurons, acting as a vital signaling molecule that supports memory formation, induces the PGC-1α/FNDC5/BDNF pathway, and enhances synaptic plasticity by potentiating NMDA glutamate receptor activity (ibidem).

Rather than supporting a simplistic, single-neurotransmitter model of mental health (such as the now-challenged serotonin theory of depression), exercise works through a dynamic, multi-system recalibration of several modulatory networks (ibidem).
• Serotonin (5-HT): Essential for emotional processing and hippocampal memory.

During sustained aerobic exercise, skeletal muscle uptake of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) frees up tryptophan to cross the BBB, boosting central 5-HT synthesis in the hippocampus, striatum, and midbrain. paired with BDNF, this supports hippocampal neurogenesis and mimics SSRI mechanisms (ibidem).
• Dopamine (DA): DA governs motivation, effort allocation, positive anticipation, and reward learning.

Acute aerobic activity lifts mood by enhancing DA synthesis and release in mesolimbic regions (nucleus accumbens and PFC), while chronic training increases D2/D3 receptor availability and density, actively repairing the brain's reward circuitry to counter anhedonia (ibidem).

• Norepinephrine (NE): Originating in the locus coeruleus, moderate exercise-induced NE elevations improve alertness and executive control in the PFC, while training recalibrates adrenergic receptor sensitivity, buffering against the hyperarousal seen in anxiety and PTSD (ibidem).
HPA axis hyperactivity (such as abnormal cortisol secretion and glucocorticoid receptor insensitivity) is a hallmark of stress-related and mood disorders (ibidem).

Chronic Adaptive Responses: While acute bouts of moderate-to-highintensity exercise trigger healthy, transient cortisol spikes to mobilize energy, chronic moderate exercise reduces resting basal cortisol, enhances glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity, and improves HPA negative-feedback efficiency.
This shifts the body toward a highly flexible, resilient stress-response system (ibidem).
Chronic low-grade inflammation (driven by pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6, TNF-a, and IL-1b) impairs neuroplasticity, reduces serotonin availability, and drives oxidative stress (ibidem).
• Systemic Anti-Inflammatory Effects: Montgomery and Grant report that regular moderate exercise has profound anti-inflammatory properties.

It downregulates Toll-like receptor expression on immune cells, increases anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10 and IL-1ra), and reduces metabolically active visceral body fat, which otherwise secretes pro-inflammatory markers (ibidem).
• The IL-6 Myokine Cascade: During acute, vigorous exercise, IL-6 is acutely synthesized and released by skeletal muscle to act as a myokine.
This acute spike initiates downstream anti-inflammatory cascades and directly inhibits TNF-a, ultimately lowering long-term baseline plasma levels of IL-6 (ibidem).
• Vagal Tone and Heart Rate Variability (HRV): Exercise improves vagal parasympathetic modulation and enhances HRV.

Crucially, an increased high frequency/low frequency ratio in HRV is positively correlated with reductions in depressive symptom severity, providing a direct physiological marker of emotional regulation (ibidem).
The Endocannabinoid System (ECS)

The endocannabinoid system, specifically the neuromodulators anandamide (AEA) and 2arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), acts as a critical biological interface regulating stress, reward, and anxiety (ibidem): • Acute Aerobic Exercise and Runner's High: The authors report that moderateintensity aerobic exercise reliably elevates circulating AEA (but not 2-AG).
This rise corresponds with reductions in pain (analgesia), diminished anxiety (anxiolysis), and elevated mood.
This is hypothesized to activate mesolimbic dopamine pathways, reinforcing exercise behavior (ibidem).
• HPA-ECS Interplay and Synaptic Plasticity: CB1 receptors on sympathetic terminals inhibit NE and CRH release, constraining excess cortisol.
Acute exerciseinduced glucocorticoid bursts upregulate 2-AG signaling in the amygdala, helping buffer emotional circuits against stress overload.
Sustained exercise also increases hippocampal CB1 receptor expression and AEA content, directly driving BDNF release and neurogenesis (ibidem).

While chronic psychological stress disrupts mitochondrial dynamics, bioenergetics, and redox balance, promoting high reactive oxygen species (ROS) and elevating psychiatric risk, exercise directly targets mitochondrial dysfunction (ibidem): • Mitochondrial Biogenesis: Aerobic exercise increases citrate synthase activity and decreases damaging ROS (ibidem).

Combining aerobic and resistance exercise amplifies skeletal muscle mitochondrial biogenesis compared to single modalities alone, enhancing ATP production and supporting overall neuroprotection (ibidem).
The psychosocial hypothesis posits that physical activity supports mental health by satisfying fundamental human psychological needs (Lubans et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The psychosocial hypothesis posits that physical activity supports mental health by satisfying fundamental human psychological needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lubans et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Lubans and colleagues identify these following needs: social interaction (relatedness), mastery in the physical domain (self-efficacy and perceived competence), improvements in appearance self-perception (body image) and independence (autonomy).
To fully unpack these psychosocial pathways, it is essential to situate them within the broader literature of sport and exercise psychology.
The psychological outcomes of movement may be heavily influenced by the motivational forces that drive behavior (Lubans et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The psychological outcomes of movement may be heavily influenced by the motivational forces that drive behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lubans et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Motivation is defined as the internal or external forces that determine the initiation, direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior (Cei, 2021).
text.formatted: Motivation is defined as the internal or external forces that determine the initiation, direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Within sport and exercise psychology, a traditional distinction is made between intrinsic motivation, where an individual engages in an activity purely for the inherent pleasure and satisfaction of the task itself and extrinsic motivation, which refers to engagement driven by instrumental goals, such as obtaining external rewards or avoiding negative consequences (Vallerand, 2007).
text.formatted: Within sport and exercise psychology, a traditional distinction is made between intrinsic motivation, where an individual engages in an activity purely for the inherent pleasure and satisfaction of the task itself and extrinsic motivation, which refers to engagement driven by instrumental goals, such as obtaining external rewards or avoiding negative consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Vallerand, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: To unify these motivational elements, Deci and Ryan (1985, 2000) formulated the Self-Determination Theory (SDT), which assumes that human beings possess an innate, proactive tendency toward psychological growth and autonomous development.
text.formatted: To unify these motivational elements, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Deci and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ryan (1985, 2000)</ref> formulated the Self-Determination Theory (SDT), which assumes that human beings possess an innate, proactive tendency toward psychological growth and autonomous development.

text.text: According to this framework, healthy psychological functioning and subjective well-being depend on the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: 1.
Competence: The need to feel effective in interacting with one's social environment and expressing one's capabilities.
Autonomy: The need to perceive oneself as the origin and author of one's own behaviors and choices.
Relatedness: The need to feel connected to others, to care and be cared for, and to experience a sense of belonging within a community.

SDT moves beyond a simple intrinsic-extrinsic dichotomy by introducing the concept of internalization, which describes a continuum of behavioral regulation ranging from nonself-determined to fully self-determined states.

This continuum spans amotivation (lack of any intent to act), externally regulated behavior (driven entirely by external rewards or punishments), introjected regulation of behavior (guided by internal pressures such as avoiding guilt, shame, or seeking approval), regulation through identification (acting out of a personal valuation of the activity's utility), integrated regulation (where the behavior is fully aligned with one's values and self-identity.
It still remains classified as extrinsic because actions are driven by personal utility rather than inherent enjoyment of the task) and finally, intrinsic motivation (Cei, 2021).
text.formatted: It still remains classified as extrinsic because actions are driven by personal utility rather than inherent enjoyment of the task) and finally, intrinsic motivation <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Deeper internalization leads to a greater sense of autonomy, which is strongly associated with enhanced well-being, high-quality performance, and long-term behavioral persistence (Moè, 2010).
text.formatted: Deeper internalization leads to a greater sense of autonomy, which is strongly associated with enhanced well-being, high-quality performance, and long-term behavioral persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Moè, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of our study, this motivational internalization provides a possible explanatory mechanism for the observed associations.

Students screening positive for mental disorders who autonomously engage in physical activity satisfy their basic psychological needs for autonomy (by choosing their active habits) and competence (by experiencing physical progress).
According to SDT, the satisfaction of these core psychological needs directly drives eudaimonic well-being.
This theoretical pathway could explain why physical activity in our cohort was strongly and independently associated with higher global life satisfaction.
A cornerstone of cognitive-behavioral functioning within sport is Albert Bandura's theory of self-efficacy, situated within the broader framework of Social Cognitive Theory (Felts, 1988).
text.formatted: A cornerstone of cognitive-behavioral functioning within sport is Albert Bandura's theory of self-efficacy, situated within the broader framework of Social Cognitive Theory <ref type="bibr">(Felts, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Self-efficacy is defined as an individual's subjective belief in their capability to successfully execute a specific task to achieve a desired outcome (Bandura, 1997).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy is defined as an individual's subjective belief in their capability to successfully execute a specific task to achieve a desired outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bandura, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, it must be distinguished from global self-esteem; while self-esteem represents a broad evaluative judgment of self-worth, self-efficacy is task-specific, though the two constructs are highly correlated and mutually reinforcing (Cei, 2021). Bandura (1997) conceptualizes self-efficacy along three essential dimensions: level (the difficulty of the tasks an individual believes they can perform), strength (the depth of conviction in one's capability), and generality (the number of life domains to which these efficacy beliefs extend) (Cei, 2021).
text.formatted: Crucially, it must be distinguished from global self-esteem; while self-esteem represents a broad evaluative judgment of self-worth, self-efficacy is task-specific, though the two constructs are highly correlated and mutually reinforcing <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bandura (1997)</ref> conceptualizes self-efficacy along three essential dimensions: level (the difficulty of the tasks an individual believes they can perform), strength (the depth of conviction in one's capability), and generality (the number of life domains to which these efficacy beliefs extend) <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: According to Bandura (1997), self-efficacy is constructed from four primary sources of information: 1.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bandura (1997)</ref>, self-efficacy is constructed from four primary sources of information: 1.

text.text: Performance Accomplishments (Mastery Experiences): The most influential source, where personal successes directly build robust efficacy beliefs, while failures undermine them.
Repeated mastery experiences can also generalize, boosting confidence in other areas where the individual previously felt inadequate.
Vicarious Experiences: Observing a competent model succeed, which is particularly effective when the model shares similar characteristics, such as gender, with the observer.
Verbal Persuasion: Encouragement or feedback from others, such as coaches, though research indicates its effects are typically modest and temporary, fading quickly after a subsequent failure.
Physiological and Affective States: The subjective interpretation of bodily arousal and somatic symptoms.

Rather than the objective level of physiological activation itself, it is the cognitive appraisal of this activation that dictates efficacy (Cei, 1998); individuals with high self-efficacy interpret somatic symptoms of arousal (such as a rapid heart rate or fatigue) as facilitative energy, whereas those with low selfefficacy interpret them as indicators of impending failure (Ibidem).
