text.text: Self-efficacy acts as a powerful cognitive mediator that shapes subsequent behavior, goal choices, emotional reactions, and cognitive appraisals (Bandura, 1977; 1997).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy acts as a powerful cognitive mediator that shapes subsequent behavior, goal choices, emotional reactions, and cognitive appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bandura, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">1997)</ref>.

text.text: Efficacy beliefs also influence how reality is subjectively filtered directly impacting emotional states and subsequent athletic and psychological outcomes (Caselli, 2024).
text.formatted: Efficacy beliefs also influence how reality is subjectively filtered directly impacting emotional states and subsequent athletic and psychological outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Caselli, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, changes in self-efficacy influence causal attributions; following a success, an increase in self-efficacy is positively correlated with internal and stable attributions, reinforcing a sense of personal agency (Ntoumanis & Biddle, 1999).
text.formatted: Furthermore, changes in self-efficacy influence causal attributions; following a success, an increase in self-efficacy is positively correlated with internal and stable attributions, reinforcing a sense of personal agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Ntoumanis & Biddle, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Within this psychosocial framework, perceived self-efficacy may act as a cognitive mediator that links physical activity to subjective well-being.

Physical activity represents a structured environment where students can experience immediate performance accomplishments (mastery experiences), which Bandura (1977; 1997) identifies as the most powerful source of self-efficacy.
text.formatted: Physical activity represents a structured environment where students can experience immediate performance accomplishments (mastery experiences), which <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bandura (1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">1997)</ref> identifies as the most powerful source of self-efficacy.

text.text: By achieving self-selected physical goals, students rebuild their task-specific confidence and physical self-worth, which can then generalize into a broader sense of global self-esteem, personal agency, and existential empowerment (Fox, 1999).
text.formatted: By achieving self-selected physical goals, students rebuild their task-specific confidence and physical self-worth, which can then generalize into a broader sense of global self-esteem, personal agency, and existential empowerment <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Fox, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: As Fox (1999) argues, taking deliberate command over one's body and movement habits triggers a broader sense of autonomy, where the primary psychological benefit is the subjective feeling of empowerment that achieving personal change provides.

This restored sense of control could weaken the cognitive foundations of hopelessness, explaining why active students in our Pavia cohort had significantly lower odds of experiencing high hopelessness.

This proposed mechanism is strongly supported by the empirical findings of Doğruyol and Tayınmak (2023), who observed that general self-efficacy is significantly and negatively correlated with hopelessness, acting as a critical cognitive mediator that buffers against psychological distress.
text.formatted: This proposed mechanism is strongly supported by the empirical findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Doğruyol and Tayınmak (2023)</ref>, who observed that general self-efficacy is significantly and negatively correlated with hopelessness, acting as a critical cognitive mediator that buffers against psychological distress.

text.text: Crucially, higher self-efficacy was found to protect individuals across all three core sub-dimensions of hopelessness: reducing negative feelings about the future, mitigating the loss of motivation, and raising positive future expectations (Doğruyol & Tayınmak, 2023).
text.formatted: Crucially, higher self-efficacy was found to protect individuals across all three core sub-dimensions of hopelessness: reducing negative feelings about the future, mitigating the loss of motivation, and raising positive future expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Doğruyol & Tayınmak, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: By illustrating that self-efficacy may serve as a vital cognitive anchor to preserve motivation and future-oriented goals, our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that movementinduced mastery experiences could help buffer the cognitive architecture of hopelessness in university students experiencing psychiatric distress.
To fully understand the psychological mechanisms behind physical activity must be conceptualized as an act of personal goal setting.
Physical activity is not merely a mechanical action.
It also represents a conscious cognitive target that a student sets for themselves (Cei, 2021).
text.formatted: It also represents a conscious cognitive target that a student sets for themselves <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: According to Edwin A. Locke's Goal-Setting Theory (1968), cognitive intentions act as a direct regulator of human action, mobilizing effort, persistence and focus.
In our Pavia cohort, higher physical activity levels were consistently associated with lower hopelessness and greater life satisfaction.
Locke's framework could provide a precise cognitive-behavioral explanation for this relationship through several key pathways, either directly or indirectly: 1.
Focus of Attention: Goals direct attention toward task-relevant activities and away from irrelevant distractions (ibidem).
For example, in distressed students, this means diverting cognitive resources away from depressive rumination or academic worry and onto concrete physical targets.
Effort: High, challenging goals mobilize greater physical and mental effort.

This process establishes a highly beneficial cyclic relationship between cognitive and motivational systems: setting clear yet challenging goals (such as performing physical activity) increases focus, which enhances task-specific performance and mastery; this achievement, in turn, boosts self-efficacy and self-esteem, motivating the individual to set further progressive goals and maintain behavioral commitment (Cei, 2021).
text.formatted: This process establishes a highly beneficial cyclic relationship between cognitive and motivational systems: setting clear yet challenging goals (such as performing physical activity) increases focus, which enhances task-specific performance and mastery; this achievement, in turn, boosts self-efficacy and self-esteem, motivating the individual to set further progressive goals and maintain behavioral commitment <ref type="bibr">(Cei, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This, in turn, could have a cascading protective effect by reducing the sense of hopelessness experience by individuals (Doğruyol and Tayınmak, 2023).
text.formatted: This, in turn, could have a cascading protective effect by reducing the sense of hopelessness experience by individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Doğruyol and Tayınmak, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, as highlighted by Emmons (2003), the specific content and cognitive orientation of a person's goals are the true determinants of subjective well-being.
text.formatted: Furthermore, as highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Emmons (2003)</ref>, the specific content and cognitive orientation of a person's goals are the true determinants of subjective well-being.

text.text: Personal goals serve as the core element of psychological organization, lending vital structure, order, and future-oriented purpose to daily life, which directly dictates how individuals evaluate their lives as meaningful and worthwhile (ibidem).
In our study, the significant associations between physical activity and elevated global life satisfaction strongly support this goal-based model of well-being.

Engaging in regular physical activity or sports represents an active commitment to intrinsic, self-selected goals, which Emmons (2003) demonstrates are robust predictors of life satisfaction and positive affect.
text.formatted: Engaging in regular physical activity or sports represents an active commitment to intrinsic, self-selected goals, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Emmons (2003)</ref> demonstrates are robust predictors of life satisfaction and positive affect.

text.text: Ultimately, integrating Emmons' framework with Locke's theory demonstrates that physical activity does not merely serve as a physiological distraction; rather, it may reorganize a student's psychological space around meaningful, attainable, and approach-oriented goals that systematically rebuild future optimism and global life satisfaction.

Sport practice can provide more potent and additional benefits through social connections and support. Eather and colleagues (2023) have identified seven mechanisms by which social support may influence mental health: -Social influence/social comparison: Group dynamics, social influence, and peer comparison can have either protective or harmful effects on an individual's mental health.
text.formatted: Sport practice can provide more potent and additional benefits through social connections and support. <ref type="bibr">Eather and colleagues (2023)</ref> have identified seven mechanisms by which social support may influence mental health: -Social influence/social comparison: Group dynamics, social influence, and peer comparison can have either protective or harmful effects on an individual's mental health.

text.text: Whether participating in individual or team sports, athletes are constantly influenced and guided by the behaviors, expectations, and norms of other players and teams.

Comparing one's own capabilities, attitudes, and values to those of other participants can directly affect an individual's behaviors and subsequent health outcomes; -Social control: This environment also involves social control, which occurs when others attempt to encourage or discourage specific health practices.
Such dynamics often manifest through strategies discussed and implemented among players, or between players and coaches.

Similarly, teammates may motivate one another to exert more effort during a match or to engage in off-field routines and events, such as fitness programs, post-game celebrations, and club gatherings, which can impact both current and future physical and mental health.
-Behavioral guidance, purpose and meaning: As seen within Locke's goal setting theory, participating in sports can offer individuals a sense of purpose, meaning, and behavioral guidance.
Through the social connections built in sports, players often develop role identities, which are defined as positions within a social structure that carry mutual duties and obligations.
In team sports especially, athletes realize they are an essential part of a larger group, giving them a shared responsibility for the team's success.

This includes concrete commitments to train, play, and communicate with the team, alongside responsibilities to maintain their own health, perform to the best of their abilities, and support their teammates.
Ultimately, because these role identities provide both direction and a sense of meaning in life, they are highly likely to impact the mental health of sports participants.
-Self-esteem: An individual's self-esteem can be deeply shaped by the social connections and support they experience through sports.
When athletes feel more capable or valued within a team environment, this localized confidence often boosts their overall self-esteem and global sense of worth.
-Sense of control: Additionally, sports offer unique opportunities to build new skills, face challenges, and develop self-control or a sense of mastery.
Actively working through and finding creative solutions to sports-related difficulties helps participants build this inner competence.
Crucially, this sense of mastery can carry over into other areas of daily life, giving individuals the confidence to handle various realworld challenges.
For instance, learning how to quickly design creative strategies against an opponent on the field can translate into greater confidence when solving creative problems in the workplace.
-Belonging and companionship: The social support and relationships built through sports can offer participants a key source of companionship and belonging.
Developing these connections, both on and off the field, with peers who share similar interests helps foster a sense of community.
Consequently, this enhanced sense of belonging may act as a mediator that leads to improved mental health outcomes.

-Perceived support availability: Social support is often provided through expressions of trust and care; instrumentally via tangible assistance; through information such as advice and suggestions; or as appraisal such feedback.
All forms of social support provided on and off the field contribute to a more generalized sense of perceived support that may mediate the effect of social interaction on mental health outcomes.
These social support mechanisms are highly relevant to the developmental stage of our sample.
Emerging adulthood is characterized by acute social and academic challenges, where students often experience isolation and a loss of structured role identities (Arnett, 2000).
text.formatted: Emerging adulthood is characterized by acute social and academic challenges, where students often experience isolation and a loss of structured role identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arnett, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings show that physical activity is a key correlate of high life satisfaction.

Through the lens of Eather and colleagues' model ( 2021), sports participation provides crucial psychosocial resources, such as role identities, behavioral guidance, and a sense of belonging, that could directly buffer against this developmental vulnerability.
text.formatted: Through the lens of Eather and colleagues' model ( <ref type="formula">2021</ref>), sports participation provides crucial psychosocial resources, such as role identities, behavioral guidance, and a sense of belonging, that could directly buffer against this developmental vulnerability.

text.text: By participating in sports, students move from feeling like isolated individuals to becoming essential parts of a social structure, transforming physical movement into a vital vehicle for interpersonal connection and global life satisfaction.

The behavioral hypothesis suggests that physical activity does not always affect mental health directly; instead, its benefits are often mediated by the adoption or optimization of other positive health behaviors (Lubans et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The behavioral hypothesis suggests that physical activity does not always affect mental health directly; instead, its benefits are often mediated by the adoption or optimization of other positive health behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lubans et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Lubans and colleagues identify these behaviors as the following: -Sleep Optimization: Physical activity plays a critical role in regulating sleep patterns by improving sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and sleep onset latency, while reducing daytime sleepiness and fatigue.
This is crucial for mental health, as insufficient sleep is heavily associated with behavioral problems and deficits in complex cognitive functioning (ibidem).
Furthermore, Lenneis and colleagues (2024) observed that a more optimized sleep pattern influence subjective well-being, which includes life satisfaction.
text.formatted: Furthermore, <ref type="bibr">Lenneis and colleagues (2024)</ref> observed that a more optimized sleep pattern influence subjective well-being, which includes life satisfaction.

text.text: -Coping Skills and Self-Regulation: Certain types of physical activity provide unique opportunities to develop cognitive, affective, and physical self-regulation.

For example, martial arts and holistic mind-body systems like yoga which integrate relaxation, mindfulness, and meditation, directly teach youth coping strategies to manage anxiety, stress, and emotional difficulties (ibidem).

Ultimately, while Eather and colleagues (2023) assert that sports participation shapes mental health through a complex, non-uniform interplay of neurobiological, psychosocial, and behavioral mechanisms, our empirical findings directly reflect this pathway heterogeneity.
Rather than producing a uniform, global shift across all health indicators, physical activity in our university cohort demonstrated more pronounced, domain-specific associations.

This is evidenced by the significant reduction in hopelessness and corresponding increases in life satisfaction, contrasted against a non-significant relationship with general self-rated mental health after full adjustment.
The observed dose-response relationship further supports the plausibility of these associations.

These findings are particularly relevant given the central role of hopelessness in the development and maintenance of mental disorders, as well as the established associations of both hopelessness and life dissatisfaction with suicidal thoughts and behaviours (Koivumaa-Honkanen et al., 2001; Yip & Cheung, 2006).
text.formatted: These findings are particularly relevant given the central role of hopelessness in the development and maintenance of mental disorders, as well as the established associations of both hopelessness and life dissatisfaction with suicidal thoughts and behaviours <ref type="bibr">(Koivumaa-Honkanen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Yip & Cheung, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions aimed at increasing physical activity among university students with mental health problems may therefore contribute not only to symptom reduction but also to fostering more positive expectations about the future.
Sedentary behaviour showed a broader pattern of association, primarily because, unlike physical activity, it remained directly related to worse self-rated mental health after adjustment.
Students reporting more than eight hours of sitting per day also had poorer outcomes across the other dimensions examined.

Our findings complement previous evidence linking sedentary behaviour to depressive and anxiety symptoms by suggesting that its associations may extend to individuals' overall appraisal of their mental health (Hallgren et al., 2018; Stanczykiewicz et al., 2019; Teychenne et al., 2015; Zhai et al., 2015).

text.text: Importantly, the associations observed in our study remained significant even after accounting for physical activity levels and other relevant covariates, supporting the notion that sedentary behaviour may exert detrimental effects beyond simply reflecting a lack of exercise.

Several mechanisms may help explain these results, including reduced social interaction, greater exposure to passive screen-based activities and the resulting disruption of sleep quality, as well as adverse neurobiological effects of prolonged sitting (Firth et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Several mechanisms may help explain these results, including reduced social interaction, greater exposure to passive screen-based activities and the resulting disruption of sleep quality, as well as adverse neurobiological effects of prolonged sitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Firth et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the association with self-rated mental health, which was not observed for physical activity after adjustment, suggests that the relationship may also include a component operating in the opposite direction, whereby poorer perceived mental health, greater symptom severity, or functional impairment may contribute to increased sedentary time.
Stratified analyses suggested that some associations of movement behaviours may extend across diagnostic profiles.

High physical activity was consistently associated with lower hopelessness across strata defined by screening status, and prolonged sedentary behaviour showed broadly adverse associations across the same strata, supporting a possible transdiagnostic relevance of these behaviours for psychological functioning.

However, this pattern was not uniform across outcomes: associations with self-rated mental health were weaker, whereas those with life satisfaction varied more substantially in magnitude and direction.
This may indicate that broader evaluations of life are more sensitive to the clinical and contextual characteristics accompanying different diagnostic profiles.
The university setting provides a particularly relevant context for these findings.

Emerging adulthood is a developmental period characterised by substantial academic, social, and psychological challenges, while mental disorders frequently emerge or become more severe during these years (Arnett, 2000; Auerbach et al., 2018; Solmi et al., 2022).

text.text: At the same time, physical activity and sedentary behaviour are modifiable behaviours that can be targeted through campus-wide health promotion initiatives (Peng et al., 2022; Plotnikoff et al., 2015).

text.text: University sport provision can encompass different forms of participation, ranging from highly competitive sport to recreational and informal physical activity (García-Álvarez & Faubel, 2020).
text.formatted: University sport provision can encompass different forms of participation, ranging from highly competitive sport to recreational and informal physical activity (García-Álvarez & Faubel, 2020).

text.text: While competitive sport can provide important social and psychological benefits (Eather et al., 2021; Cei, 2021), performance-oriented environments may also expose participants to additional pressures, including training demands and competitive stress (Rice et al., 2016).

text.text: Conversely, research on campus recreation suggests that participation is influenced by a range of interpersonal and structural barriers, including accessibility, social connections and familiarity with available opportunities (Sim et al., 2026; Selvaratnam et al., 2021).

text.text: This suggests that simply providing sporting opportunities may not be sufficient to engage less-active students, particularly those who do not identify with competitive sport.

Universities may therefore benefit from adopting a broader approach to physical-activity promotion, alongside competitive sport, that emphasizes accessible and inclusive opportunities for students with different levels of ability, motivation and experience.
To encourage broader student participation in physical activity, institutions could leverage the existing academic credit system.
Research has examined the use of academic incentives to promote physical activity among students, suggesting that such incentives may increase participation (DeVahl et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Research has examined the use of academic incentives to promote physical activity among students, suggesting that such incentives may increase participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(DeVahl et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, greater academic incentives were associated with greater intervention effectiveness, as reflected in both higher exercise adherence and improved health outcomes (ibidem).

Whitin the Italian university system, this could be operationalized by awarding university credits (CFUs) for sports participation, or alternatively, by establishing a mandatory physical activity CFU quota within degree requirements.

Additionally, for universities lacking dedicated on-campus fitness facilities, institutions could forge private-sector partnerships with local gyms to offer students subsidized, reduced-rate training options (Sim et al., 2026).

text.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions regarding causality or directionality.
Although early models conceptualized the association as primarily unidirectional (PA → MH) (Biddle, 2016), more recent research suggests a bidirectional relationship.
text.formatted: Although early models conceptualized the association as primarily unidirectional (PA → MH) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Biddle, 2016)</ref>, more recent research suggests a bidirectional relationship.

text.text: While exercise can improve mental wellbeing, individuals with better mental health are more likely to engage in regular physical activity (Ahsan & Abualait, 2025).
text.formatted: While exercise can improve mental wellbeing, individuals with better mental health are more likely to engage in regular physical activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ahsan & Abualait, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, all measures were self-reported and may therefore be subject to recall bias and reporting inaccuracies.
Third, mental disorders were identified using validated screening instruments rather than clinical diagnoses.
Finally, the study was conducted within a single Italian university, which may limit the generalisability of findings to other educational and cultural contexts.

Despite these limitations, the study has several important strengths, including the large sample size, the use of validated instruments within the WMH-ICS framework, the simultaneous consideration of both physical activity and sedentary behaviour, the focus on subjective outcomes that are highly relevant to the everyday experience of students living with mental disorders, and the capability of taking into account several potential confounders in the regression models.

To our knowledge, few studies have examined how movement behaviours relate to self-rated mental health, life satisfaction, and hopelessness specifically among university students screening positive for mental disorders.
In conclusion, physical activity and sedentary behaviour were differentially associated with how students experienced living with a mental disorder.

Higher physical activity was most consistently associated with lower hopelessness and greater life satisfaction, whereas prolonged sedentary time was associated with poorer outcomes across all dimensions, including self-rated mental health.

Although a component operating in the opposite direction cannot be excluded, these findings identify movement behaviours as potentially modifiable targets and accessible markers of students experiencing less favourable outcomes.
Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to establish temporal direction and determine whether increasing physical activity and reducing sedentary time can improve these outcomes.
